questions.title: Controlled-Z and basis change
questions.prompt: Task 10: Build a circuit using cz, and show it behaves like a CNOT conjugated by Hadamards.
questions.starterCode:
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
# H on target, cz, H on target
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cz(0, 1)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: H-CZ-H on the target is exactly CNOT. Control and target are basis-dependent labels, not physical roles — the same interaction looks different in a different basis.

questions.title: Parameterised single-qubit ansatz
questions.prompt: Task 1: Build a one-qubit ansatz with Ry(theta) for theta = pi/4 and measure it.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(1, 1)
circuit.ry(0, math.pi / 4)
circuit.measure(0, 0)
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: An ansatz is a circuit with tunable parameters. The optimiser's whole job is choosing theta; here you are seeing one fixed point in that search space.

questions.title: Two-parameter ansatz
questions.prompt: Task 2: Build a 2-qubit ansatz applying Ry(pi/3) to qubit 0 and Ry(pi/6) to qubit 1.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.ry(0, math.pi / 3)
circuit.ry(1, math.pi / 6)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Parameter count grows with qubits, which is why VQE ansatz design matters — too many parameters and the classical optimiser cannot navigate the landscape.

questions.title: Hardware-efficient ansatz with entanglement
questions.prompt: Task 3: Build a layer of Ry rotations followed by a CNOT entangling layer on 2 qubits.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.ry(0, math.pi / 4)
circuit.ry(1, math.pi / 4)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Rotation layer then entangling layer is the hardware-efficient pattern. Without the CNOT the ansatz can only reach product states, so it could never represent a correlated ground state.

questions.title: QAOA mixing layer
questions.prompt: Task 4: Build the QAOA starting state — equal superposition over 3 qubits — then apply an Rx mixer.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(3, 3)
for i in range(3):
    circuit.h(i)
for i in range(3):
    circuit.rx(math.pi / 4, i)
circuit.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: QAOA alternates a cost layer and a mixer. The mixer (Rx) moves amplitude between candidate solutions so the optimiser is not stuck at its starting point.

questions.title: MaxCut cost layer
questions.prompt: Task 5: Apply a ZZ interaction between qubits 0 and 1 using two CNOTs and an Rz.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.rz(1, math.pi / 2)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: CNOT-Rz-CNOT implements exp(-i*theta*ZZ), the cost term for one MaxCut edge. Every edge in the graph contributes one of these.

questions.title: Angle encoding
questions.prompt: Task 1: Encode the classical value 0.5 into a qubit using Ry(2*0.5) — angle encoding.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(1, 1)
circuit.ry(0, 2 * 0.5)
circuit.measure(0, 0)
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Angle encoding maps a number onto a rotation. One qubit carries one feature, so the qubit count scales with your feature count — the main constraint on near-term QML.

questions.title: Encoding a two-feature sample
questions.prompt: Task 2: Encode the vector [0.3, 0.8] into two qubits by angle encoding.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.ry(0, 2 * 0.3)
circuit.ry(1, 2 * 0.8)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Each feature gets its own qubit. The measured distribution differs per sample, which is what makes the encoding informative to a downstream classifier.

questions.title: Feature map with entanglement
questions.prompt: Task 3: Encode two features, then entangle them with a CNOT to build a non-linear feature map.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.ry(0, 2 * 0.3)
circuit.ry(1, 2 * 0.8)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Entangling after encoding creates feature interactions a linear model cannot represent. This is the quantum analogue of a kernel trick.

questions.title: Variational classifier circuit
questions.prompt: Task 4: Build encode -> entangle -> trainable rotation, the standard QML classifier shape.
questions.solution:
import math
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.ry(0, 2 * 0.3)
circuit.ry(1, 2 * 0.8)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.ry(0, math.pi / 3)
circuit.ry(1, math.pi / 5)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Data goes in via fixed rotations; the trainable weights are separate rotations after entangling. Only the second set is optimised during training.

questions.title: Swap test for state overlap
questions.prompt: Task 5: Build a swap test using a control qubit, Hadamard, controlled-swap and Hadamard.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(3, 1)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.x(1)
circuit.cswap(0, 1, 2)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.measure(0, 0)
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: The swap test measures how similar two states are: P(control=0) = (1 + |<a|b>|^2)/2. Identical states always give 0; orthogonal ones give 50/50. This is the quantum kernel.

questions.title: Prepare the shared Bell pair
questions.prompt: Task 1: Build the entangled pair shared between sender and receiver, on qubits 1 and 2.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(3, 3)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Teleportation needs a Bell pair distributed in advance. Qubit 0 stays free to carry the message; qubits 1 and 2 are the shared resource.

questions.title: Prepare the message qubit
questions.prompt: Task 2: Put the message qubit (qubit 0) into the |+> state before teleporting it.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(3, 3)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: The message can be any state. |+> is a good test because it is not a basis state — if teleportation only worked for |0> and |1> it would just be classical communication.

questions.title: Bell measurement
questions.prompt: Task 3: Perform the sender's Bell measurement — CNOT from message to her half, then Hadamard.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(3, 3)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: The Bell measurement entangles the message with the shared pair and then reads it out. This destroys the original — no-cloning is respected, not circumvented.

questions.title: Full teleportation circuit
questions.prompt: Task 4: Assemble the complete protocol: prepare, entangle, Bell-measure, correct.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(3, 3)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.h(1)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.cx(1, 2)
circuit.cz(0, 2)
circuit.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: The final CNOT and CZ apply the corrections the receiver would make after hearing the two classical bits. Those two bits are why teleportation cannot beat light speed.

questions.title: Superdense coding
questions.prompt: Task 5: Build superdense coding — send two classical bits using one qubit and prior entanglement.
questions.solution:
circuit = Circuit(2, 2)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.x(0)
circuit.z(0)
circuit.cx(0, 1)
circuit.h(0)
circuit.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
job_result = circuit.run(shots=1024)
counts = job_result.get_counts()
print(counts)
questions.explanation: Superdense coding is teleportation run backwards: one qubit carries two classical bits, given a pre-shared Bell pair. Applying X and Z encodes the bit pair 11.
